summary: The city council has announced a Parks and Playgrounds Upgrade program starting September 15, 2023, aimed at making public spaces more inclusive, sustainable, tech-enabled, and safe. Planners are using community feedback and private sponsorship, with features like accessible play equipment, native plants, Wi-Fi zones, improved security, and local business kiosks. Officials and consultants describe it as a reimagining of community spaces for the 21st century.
one_line: The city's Parks and Playgrounds Upgrade, starting September 15, 2023, will make parks more inclusive, green, smart, safe, and supportive of local business.
key_facts: The city council's Parks and Playgrounds Upgrade program is slated to commence on September 15, 2023.
The upgrades are spearheaded by city planners and backed by a consortium of private sponsors.
Chief urban planner Jared Emerson said the initiative is about making parks more inclusive, safer, and aligned with residents' activities, using smart technology and eco-friendly designs.
The city has opened a platform for citizens to share their visions for parks as part of a collaborative design pilot.
Rebecca Thompson, a local mother of two, called for playground equipment accessible to children with different abilities.
Proposed designs include sensory-friendly zones and wheelchair-accessible play structures.
Eco-features include native plants, pollinator gardens, rainwater harvesting systems, and solar-powered lighting.
Landscape architect Marissa Grant said "Eco-friendly should be the norm, not an afterthought."
Smart parks will feature free Wi-Fi zones, charging stations, and interactive digital play surfaces.
Tech consultant Aaron Lee, engaged by the council, says tech in parks can help bridge the digital divide and encourage older generations to become more tech-literate.
A significant portion of the upgrade budget is allocated to security, including improved lighting, surveillance systems, and emergency response tools.
Accessibility measures include visible pathways and ramps, tactile signs for the visually impaired, and auditory signals at crossings.
Safety consultant Juliana Keech said "We're not waiting for accidents to happen. We're working to prevent them."
The proposal includes small business kiosks, farmer's markets, and art installations by local artisans to stimulate the local economy.
Economic strategist Derrick O'Connor said the spaces will help local entrepreneurs build a self-sustaining ecosystem.
